clue.text: Commotion in British (or French) ditch

parts.note: the bracket says 'or' in French, which is the word ou
a ha-ha is a sunken ditch serving as a hidden fence round a park

explanation.surface: Somebody is puzzling over what to call a trench on either side of the Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket '(or French)' asks for the French word for 'or', OU. A HA-HA is a ditch with a wall in it, a feature of English country-house gardens.
explanation.definitionFit: A noisy fuss or uproar is a commotion, a synonym pair.

clue.text: Church supporting platform for Ambrose

indicators.note: in a down clue, the piece that supports another sits beneath it

parts.note: a bier is a platform on which a coffin rests
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A church holds up a platform for someone named Ambrose.
explanation.walkthrough: Ambrose Bierce, the American writer of The Devil's Dictionary, is defined by his first name; 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambrose Bierce was the American satirist, so his surname follows the first name given.

clue.text: Base authority is won from their books, thought Biron "

definitions.text: Base authority is won from their books, thought Biron

parts.words: Base authority is won from their books, thought Biron
parts.note: in Love's Labour's Lost Biron scorns plodding scholars who gain only 'base authority from ...' books, meaning the books of other people

explanation.walkthrough: Biron, in Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost, says plodders win 'save base authority from others' books'; the clue paraphrases that line.
explanation.definitionFit: Biron's line is about the books of other people, so the answer names those people, everyone else.

clue.text: "You cataracts and -es spout" (King Lear)

parts.note: Lear in the storm calls on 'cataracts and ...es' to spout, a gap for an old form of the word for a violent tropical storm

explanation.walkthrough: In the storm scene of King Lear the king cries 'Blow, winds... You cataracts and hurricanoes, spout'; the clue leaves the word stem blank and the count gives its length.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's old spelling of a violent tropical cyclone, used as Lear calls on the waterspouts of the storm.

clue.text: He saw it through, thanks to H. G. Wells

definitions.text: He saw it through, thanks to H. G. Wells

parts.words: He saw it through, thanks to H. G. Wells
parts.note: H. G. Wells wrote the novel Mr Britling Sees It Through, about an English writer living through the First World War

explanation.walkthrough: The title Mr Britling Sees It Through is the hint; the solver supplies the hero's full name, first name included.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Wells's 1916 novel is a writer who endures the war years, giving his full name.

clue.text: "God is the last fading smile of a cheshire cat" (Sir Julian Huxley)

definitions.text: "God is the last fading smile of a cheshire cat" (Sir Julian Huxley)

parts.words: "God is the last fading smile of a cheshire cat" (Sir Julian Huxley)
parts.note: a quotation with a word left out: Huxley's line describes the Cheshire cat as belonging to the whole universe, and the missing adjective fills that gap

explanation.walkthrough: Huxley's full line reads 'the last fading smile of a cosmic Cheshire cat'; the solver supplies the omitted adjective, and the count gives its length.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing adjective means universal, relating to the whole of the universe, which is what Huxley's cat smiles across.

clue.text: Palinurus claimed that it made de Quincey great and Cocteau serious

definitions.text: Palinurus claimed that it made de Quincey great and Cocteau serious

parts.words: Palinurus claimed that it made de Quincey great and Cocteau serious
parts.note: Palinurus was Cyril Connolly's pen name for The Unquiet Grave; both de Quincey and Cocteau wrote about their addiction to a poppy drug

explanation.walkthrough: Palinurus is the pen name Cyril Connolly used for The Unquiet Grave. De Quincey wrote Confessions of an English Opium-Eater and Cocteau wrote a journal of his cure.
explanation.definitionFit: The narcotic drawn from poppies was taken by both de Quincey and Cocteau, each of whom wrote about it.

clue.text: Kipling's poetic symbol of the self with unknown quantity

definitions.note: short for Kipling's poetic place, a poem title naming a Burmese city

parts.note: Jung took the mandala, a circular design, as a symbol of the whole self
in algebra y, like x, stands for an unknown quantity

explanation.surface: Kipling's verse treats the self as a symbol plus an unknown quantity.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's poem is titled after the Burmese city; the def is elliptical for 'Kipling's poetic place'. 'With' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling wrote the poem about the road to this Burmese city, the old royal capital of Burma.

clue.text: Alice's acquaintances are meant to be taken on board

definitions.meaning: in Through the Looking-Glass Alice meets the Red and White Kings and Queens, pieces from a game

definitions.text: meant to be taken on board
definitions.meaning: the pieces of the game of kings and queens are played and captured on a board

explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken on board' sounds like accepting an idea, but it means captured on a chequered board.
explanation.definitionFit: The pieces of the game played on a chequered board are what Alice meets in Looking-Glass Land, and they are captured during play.

clue.text: Dramatist shows anaesthetic, for example, to the point

parts.note: ether was an early general anaesthetic
e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, for example
E is a point of the compass, east

explanation.surface: A playwright stages a scene with anaesthetic gas, a fine illustration that goes straight to the point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shows' and 'to' are link words; 'the point' is a compass point, E. Sir George Etherege was a Restoration comic dramatist.
explanation.definitionFit: George Etherege wrote Restoration comedies such as The Man of Mode, so he is a playwright.

clue.text: She spent Happy Days with a sand castle, so to speak

definitions.text: She spent Happy Days with a sand castle, so to speak

parts.words: She spent Happy Days with a sand castle, so to speak
parts.note: Beckett's play Happy Days shows its heroine buried to the waist, then the neck, in a mound of earth, a kind of sand castle on the stage

explanation.walkthrough: Happy Days reads like a seaside holiday, but it is Samuel Beckett's play; its central character spends the whole piece sunk in a mound.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Beckett's Happy Days is a woman named for this character, chattering while embedded in a heap.

clue.text: What Simon created strangely helped Doc out

indicators.note: strangely means in an odd way, so the letters of the words that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: Simon behaved oddly when he helped a doctor get away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' looks like part of the phrase 'helped Doc out', and it is: all three words are the fodder for 'strangely'. Simon is the playwright Neil Simon.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil Simon wrote the comedy about two mismatched flatmates, a play he created.

clue.text: Dog-eared paperback?

parts.note: read literally, a paperback from a publisher named after a breed of dog with large pointed ears; the surface suggests a worn book

explanation.walkthrough: Dog-eared normally means a book with folded page corners; here it points to a paperback imprint that took its name and logo from a small Welsh dog breed.
explanation.definitionFit: Corgi Books is a British paperback imprint named after the short-legged Welsh herding dog.

clue.text: Murger's operatic prototypes

parts.note: Henri Murger's Scenes de la vie de boheme gave Puccini the characters of his opera La Boheme

explanation.walkthrough: Henri Murger wrote sketches of poor Paris artists that became the source of Puccini's La Boheme, so his characters are the originals of the opera's figures.
explanation.definitionFit: Murger's sketches portray penniless Parisian artists living unconventionally, the original free-living types.

clue.text: Easily croon a medley in gambling venue

indicators.note: a medley is a jumble of tunes, so the singer's words are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A lounge singer gently croons a string of songs in the casino.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A medley' is the anagram signal, and the fodder 'Easily croon a' takes the clue's earlier 'a' with it; 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian Fleming's first Bond novel is named after a fictional casino, a place where people gamble.

clue.text: Podally challenged, like the cook of the Hispaniola

definitions.meaning: a jokey euphemism for having a missing foot or leg

definitions.text: like the cook of the Hispaniola
definitions.meaning: in Stevenson's Treasure Island the ship's cook Long John Silver has a wooden leg

explanation.walkthrough: The Hispaniola is the ship in Treasure Island; its cook is Long John Silver, who walks on a crutch.
explanation.definitionFit: Long John Silver lost a limb, so he is physically short of a lower limb, a state the jokey euphemism describes.

clue.text: She was finally trained by Tolstoy

definitions.text: She was finally trained by Tolstoy

parts.words: She was finally trained by Tolstoy
parts.note: Tolstoy's heroine Anna ends her life under a railway train, so 'trained' is a grim pun on her death

explanation.walkthrough: 'Trained' suggests schooling, but Tolstoy's heroine dies throwing herself under a train; the answer is her surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolstoy's heroine Anna dies beneath a train at the novel's end, and this is her married surname.

clue.text: Kit's ploy upset the chaplain

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters of Kit's ploy are rearranged

explanation.surface: Kit's scheme annoyed the army padre.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'Kit's' is ignored and its S is part of the fodder. The answer is slang for a military chaplain.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a clergyman, especially a forces padre, a chaplain who guides souls heavenward.

clue.text: Admitted (universally) like Jane's well known truth

definitions.meaning: Jane Austen opens Pride and Prejudice with 'It is a truth universally ...', the famous truth everybody concedes

explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed 'universally' joins both halves: Austen's first sentence calls the truth universally conceded.
explanation.definitionFit: To admit something is to recognise it as true, and Austen's opening line describes a truth that everyone recognises.

clue.text: His employers experienced a close shave in Spain

definitions.text: His employers experienced a close shave in Spain

parts.words: His employers experienced a close shave in Spain
parts.note: the Barber of Seville literally gives his clients a close shave, while the phrase sounds like a narrow escape

explanation.walkthrough: A close shave usually means a narrow escape; here it is literal, because Beaumarchais's hero is the Barber of Seville.
explanation.definitionFit: Beaumarchais's Barber of Seville, made famous by Rossini, shaves his clients in Spain.

clue.text: Porpoise has ego problems

indicators.note: having problems suggests the letters of has ego are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A dolphin-like creature turns out to have issues with its self-esteem.
explanation.definitionFit: An old name for the porpoise, a small toothed whale likened to a pig of the sea.

clue.text: Clumsily personate lingua franca

indicators.note: done clumsily means done awkwardly, so the letters of personate are jumbled

explanation.surface: An actor impersonates someone badly while speaking a common tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: Zamenhof's invented language was meant as an international common tongue, a lingua franca for speakers of different languages.

clue.text: Positivist Academician glimpsed in barren Annecy landscape

indicators.note: glimpsed in says the answer can be caught sight of within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A French philosopher is spotted on a walk through bare country near a lake in Savoy.
explanation.walkthrough: Ernest Renan, French historian of religion and member of the Academie francaise, was associated with positivism; Annecy is a town in the French Alps.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest Renan was a French scholar elected to the Academie francaise and influenced by positivist thought.

clue.text: Chosen part of novel item

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A selected passage forms one section of a novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The select few, the best of a group, are those picked out, as an adjective meaning chosen.

clue.text: Gulliver left one rather up in the air

definitions.text: Gulliver left one rather up in the air

parts.words: Gulliver left one rather up in the air
parts.note: in Gulliver's Travels the flying land of Laputa floats overhead, so a place Gulliver left really was up in the air

explanation.walkthrough: 'Up in the air' sounds like uncertainty, but Swift's Laputa is literally airborne, a floating land that Gulliver visits and leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Laputa is a land mass surrounded by sky rather than sea, a flying piece of land.

clue.text: Quote for unreliable pie-chart

indicators.note: an unreliable word cannot be trusted to stay as it is, so the letters of pie are jumbled

parts.note: a graph is a chart

explanation.surface: Someone warns that a pie-chart cannot be trusted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unreliable' scrambles only 'pie', making EPI; the hyphenated 'pie-chart' looks like one item but splits in two. 'For' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: An inscription or a quotation set at the head of a book or chapter is a quote of this kind.

clue.text: He came "smiling from the world's great snare uncaught"

definitions.text: He came "smiling from the world's great snare uncaught"

parts.words: He came "smiling from the world's great snare uncaught"
parts.note: Cleopatra greets her returning lover with these words in Shakespeare's tragedy, after he comes back victorious from battle

explanation.walkthrough: The line is Cleopatra's in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra, Act 4, welcoming the Roman general home from fighting Caesar.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleopatra addresses these words to her Roman lover Mark, the general returning from battle.

clue.text: Hasty creation of Peacock

definitions.meaning: Thomas Love Peacock wrote the satirical novel ... Hall, with its Squire of that name

explanation.walkthrough: Peacock is not a bird here but the novelist Thomas Love Peacock.
explanation.definitionFit: Rushing in rashly is acting precipitately, and Peacock's Squire of Headlong Hall bears that surname.
